name: Site Answers – MCP Server, llms.txt & AI Crawler Log
author: PinMaster

sections.description:
AI assistants are reading your website. Site Answers has one job: make your site
readable to them, show you whether they actually came, let you decide which of them
may, and let the AI agents you choose search and read it directly. These parts make a
WordPress site agent-ready, and together they are the whole plugin.

It is a read-only MCP server for AI agents. MCP, the Model Context Protocol, is the
standard way AI assistants such as Claude, ChatGPT and Cursor connect to tools. Make a token
under Site Answers → AI Agents (MCP), give your agent the address and the token, and it can
search your published posts and pages and read any of them as clean Markdown. It gets four
tools: search_content, get_post, list_recent and get_site_info. It cannot change
anything: there are no write tools at all, not even switched-off ones. Each token is
revocable and limited to 60 calls a minute, and the access log shows which token used which
tool on which page, and when. If your site runs WordPress’s official MCP Adapter plugin, the
same four tools are registered as WordPress abilities too, so its agents get them with no
token at all.

It publishes an llms.txt file. llms.txt is an emerging convention — a plain,
readable Markdown index at the root of your site that tells AI assistants what you
have published and where to find it. Site Answers builds yours from your own posts and
pages: your site name, your tagline, then one line per URL with its title and a short
description. It is rebuilt automatically whenever you publish, edit or delete
something, so it never goes stale.

It publishes llms-full.txt too. Where llms.txt is the map, llms-full.txt is the
whole territory: the full text of every page llms.txt lists, one after another, in one file,
so an AI assistant can read your site in a single visit. Same pages, same exclusions, capped at
5 MB with a note saying where the rest is. You can switch it off in Settings.

It logs which AI crawlers visit. GPTBot, ClaudeBot, PerplexityBot, OAI-SearchBot,
CCBot and the others are recognised by name. For each visit you see which crawler
came, which page it asked for, and whether it got the page or an error. That answers a
question site owners currently cannot answer at all: is AI search actually reading my
content, and which pages does it want?

It serves a clean Markdown copy of every page. Add .md to the end of any post or page
address and you get the article as plain Markdown — headings, paragraphs, lists, links and
tables — with the navigation, sidebars, share buttons and scripts left out. That is what an
automated reader wants, and it is far less likely to be misquoted than a page it had to dig out
of a theme. Each HTML page also advertises its Markdown twin in a Link header, so a crawler
can find it without guessing.

It tells you when your robots.txt is turning AI crawlers away. An empty crawler log often
has a simple cause: a line in robots.txt — added by another plugin, a host, or years ago by
hand — asking GPTBot or ClaudeBot to stay away. The Overview reads the robots.txt your site
actually serves, the way the crawlers read it, and names every AI crawler it blocks.

And it lets you choose, crawler by crawler. In Settings, each AI crawler has three
choices: No change, Allow or Block. Block ChatGPT’s training crawler and keep the one that
fetches your page when someone asks ChatGPT about you, or the other way round. Your choices go
into WordPress’s own robots.txt. Until you pick something, robots.txt stays exactly as it was.

How this is different

Plenty of plugins will write an llms.txt for you. Almost all of them stop at that point: the
file is written, and you never find out whether anything read it. This one closes the loop — it
publishes the file, serves your pages in a form a machine can actually read, and then shows you
whether any AI crawler turned up and what it asked for. Publishing without measuring is
guesswork, and until now measuring meant reading raw server logs.

The same goes for MCP. Many MCP plugins hand an agent your whole WordPress through an
application password, which can do anything that user can, writing included. This one is
read-only by construction, its tokens can do exactly one thing and are revoked in one click,
and every tool returns the same clean Markdown text the .md addresses serve, not raw page
HTML for the agent to dig through.

Three further differences, each of which you can check in the code:

  • It stands aside rather than fighting for the address. If another plugin, or a static file
    in your web root, already serves /llms.txt, Site Answers never registers its own route for it:
    theirs keeps working untouched, and your settings screen tells you which one is answering. Two
    plugins answering one address is how sites break, and it is always the newer plugin that gets
    blamed for it.
  • It keeps nothing personal. The crawler log holds the crawler’s name, the page path, the
    response status and the time. No IP addresses, no query strings, no headers — so it never grows
    into a consent-banner problem the way a general-purpose visitor log does.
  • It asks for nothing. No account, no API key, no external service, no outbound request of
    any kind, and nothing to upgrade to. Everything happens on your own server, so nothing about
    your site or your visitors leaves it.

What it does not do

This plugin does not connect to any external service. It makes no outbound HTTP request
of any kind — no API, no phone-home, no telemetry, no analytics, no third-party
libraries. Everything it shows you was produced by your own site, on your own server.
AI agents you connect over MCP send requests to your site; your site never contacts them.

It stores no IP addresses. The crawler log records the crawler’s name, the page path and
the time — nothing else. The MCP access log records the token (or the WordPress user), the
tool, the page read or the words searched, and the time. Anything after the ? in an address is discarded before the
record is written, because query strings on real sites carry e-mail addresses, order
references and reset tokens. Records older than 90 days are deleted automatically.

It changes nothing on its own. Your robots.txt is left exactly as it is until you choose
Allow or Block for a crawler, and no file is ever written to your server: if you have a
robots.txt file of your own, the plugin tells you so and leaves it alone.

Why this matters

AI assistants increasingly answer questions using content they read from websites, and being
readable to them is becoming its own discipline — answer engine optimization, or AEO, alongside
the generative engine optimization people now talk about next to ordinary SEO. Both come down
to the same two practical questions: can a large language model find and parse what you
published, and is it actually doing so? Site Answers gives you a straight answer to the second
one, and does the groundwork for the first.

Who it is for

Anyone who publishes writing and wants to know whether AI search engines are reading it.
Bloggers, documentation sites, shops with real content, agencies who need to show a
client what is happening.

Privacy

No personal data of any kind is collected, stored or transmitted. Because no IP address
is recorded and nothing leaves your server, this plugin does not put your site into
consent-banner territory.
sections.installation:
1. Install and activate the plugin.
  2. Visit Site Answers → Overview. Your llms.txt link is at the top.
  3. Optionally visit Site Answers → Settings to choose which content is listed and which AI crawlers may read your site.
  4. To let an AI agent read your site over MCP, visit Site Answers → AI Agents (MCP), make a token, and paste the address and the token into your agent. The screen shows a ready-made command and configuration to copy.

There is nothing to sign up for. The MCP tokens are made on your own site and never leave it unless you give one to an agent.
sections.faq:
What is llms.txt?

It is a proposed convention — like robots.txt or sitemap.xml, but written for large
language models. A single Markdown file at /llms.txt that tells an AI assistant what a
site contains, in a form it can read without wading through navigation, adverts and
scripts. It is young and not every AI engine reads it yet, which is exactly why it costs
almost nothing to publish one now.

Where is my llms.txt?

At /llms.txt on your site, and the Overview screen links straight to it.

What is llms-full.txt?

The companion to llms.txt. Instead of a list of links, it holds the full text of every page
llms.txt lists, as Markdown, in one file at /llms-full.txt. Each page starts with its title
and a Source: line with its address. It leaves out exactly what llms.txt leaves out —
drafts, private and password-protected posts, and pages marked “noindex” — and stops at 5 MB.
On a large site the first visit may not include every page yet: pages are converted a few at a
time so the file never times out, and the file says so when that happens.

My llms.txt says “not found”. Why?

Almost always because Settings → Reading → “Discourage search engines from indexing
this site” is switched on. Site Answers honours that: if you have asked search engines
to stay away, it does not publish an index of your content on your behalf. The Overview
screen tells you when this is the reason. Switch that setting off and the file appears
immediately.

If that setting is already off, something else is probably answering at that address: a
static llms.txt file in your site’s root folder, or another plugin that publishes one.
Site Answers steps aside for both rather than fight over the address, and the Overview
screen names whichever it is.

Which AI crawlers are detected?

GPTBot, OAI-SearchBot and ChatGPT-User (OpenAI); ClaudeBot, Claude-User and anthropic-ai
(Anthropic); PerplexityBot and Perplexity-User (Perplexity); Google-Extended and
GoogleOther (Google); CCBot (Common Crawl); Bytespider (ByteDance); Amazonbot (Amazon);
Applebot-Extended (Apple); Meta-ExternalAgent (Meta); cohere-ai (Cohere); DuckAssistBot
(DuckDuckGo); YouBot (You.com); and Diffbot.

Google-Extended and Applebot-Extended are robots.txt names only: Google and Apple fetch pages
with their ordinary crawlers and use these names to let you opt out of AI training. They can
be blocked in Settings, but they never appear in the visit log.

How do I get the Markdown version of a page?

Add .md to the end of its address. A post at https://example.com/hello-world/ is also
served at https://example.com/hello-world.md. The HTML page carries a
Link: <…>; rel=”alternate”; type=”text/markdown” header pointing at it, which is how an
automated reader is meant to discover it.

Drafts, private posts, password-protected posts and anything you have marked “noindex”
are not served this way, exactly as they are kept out of llms.txt. The Markdown copy
also carries X-Robots-Tag: noindex and a canonical link back to the real page, so it
cannot compete with your own article in search results.

What is MCP, and how do I connect an AI agent to my site?

MCP, the Model Context Protocol, is the open standard AI assistants use to connect to tools
and data. Site Answers turns your site into a read-only MCP server:

  1. Go to Site Answers → AI Agents (MCP) and make a token. Give it a name you will
    recognise, such as “Claude on my laptop”.
  2. Copy the token straight away: it is shown once, and only a fingerprint of it is kept.
  3. Give your agent the MCP server address shown on that screen (it ends in
    /wp-json/site-answers/v1/mcp) and send the token as Authorization: Bearer <token>. The
    screen has a ready-made Claude Code command and a JSON block for clients such as Cursor and
    VS Code that take an address and headers.

The agent then has four tools: search_content (search your posts and pages),
get_post (read one in full, as Markdown, by id or address), list_recent (the newest
content) and get_site_info (your site’s name, language, content types and llms.txt
address).

Can an AI agent change my site through MCP?

No. There are no write tools: the code to create, edit or delete anything does not exist
in this plugin, so there is nothing a token, a bug or a setting could switch on. A token can
read what your llms.txt lists and nothing else, and revoking it stops it on its very next
call.

Which content can an agent read?

Exactly what llms.txt lists: the content types ticked in Settings, published, with no
password, and nothing marked “noindex” by your SEO plugin. Drafts, private posts and
password-protected posts are never reachable, even through an administrator’s agent. The
siteanswers_mcp_exclude_post filter withholds any other post in code. The “Discourage
search engines” setting does not close the MCP server, because a token is you personally
giving your own agent a key.

Does it work with the WordPress MCP Adapter?

Yes. On WordPress 6.9 and newer the four tools are also registered with WordPress’s
Abilities API as site-answers/search-content, site-answers/get-post,
site-answers/list-recent and site-answers/get-site-info. If you use the official MCP
Adapter plugin, its agents find them with no further setup, signed in as a WordPress user
rather than with a Site Answers token, and their calls appear in the same access log. You
can switch this off in Settings.

My agent gets “401” or “unauthorized”. What now?

Check that the token is sent as Authorization: Bearer <token> and has not been revoked.
If it is right and still refused, your host may be dropping the Authorization header before
WordPress sees it. This happens on some Apache servers, and adding
SetEnvIf Authorization “(.*)” HTTP_AUTHORIZATION=$1 to your .htaccess fixes it. A security
plugin that blocks the WordPress REST API for logged-out visitors will also block the MCP
address; allow site-answers/v1 in its settings.

Is there a limit on how much an agent can read?

Each token may make 60 tool calls a minute, which is plenty for an agent researching your
site and stops a runaway one from loading your server. A page longer than 100 KB of text is
cut there, and the agent is told so.

Does this plugin send anything to anyone?

No. It makes no outbound HTTP request at all. There is no account, no API key, no
telemetry and no analytics of any kind. AI agents you connect over MCP send requests to your
site; your site never contacts them.

The Overview and AI Agents (MCP) screens carry one ordinary link, “Get early access”, to a
page about a possible paid add-on. Nothing is sent when a screen loads; the page opens in your
browser only if you click, and your e-mail address reaches us only if you type it there.

Is there a paid version?

Not yet. Everything described here is free and stays free. We are considering an optional
paid add-on that answers your visitors’ questions from your own content; the “Get early
access” link on the Overview and AI Agents (MCP) screens lets you ask to be told if it is built. It is never
shown as a notice, and nothing in this plugin is locked behind it.

Does it record IP addresses?

No. The crawler name, the page path and the time — that is the whole record. Query
strings are discarded too. The MCP access log stores no IP address either: only the token
or WordPress user, the tool, the page read or the words searched, and the time.

My server log shows more AI crawler visits than this plugin does. Why?

If your site uses full-page caching — nginx FastCGI cache, WP Rocket, Cloudflare, a host
level cache — then a cached page is served without WordPress running at all, so the
plugin never sees that visit. This is true of every WordPress-level bot log, not just
this one. Treat the numbers here as a floor rather than a total.

Does it work with my SEO plugin?

Yes. If a page is marked “noindex” in Yoast SEO, Rank Math, SEOPress or The SEO
Framework, Site Answers leaves it out of llms.txt by default. You can turn that off in
Settings. For any other rule, the siteanswers_llms_txt_exclude_post filter lets you
exclude a page in code.

Will it list my drafts or private posts?

No. Only published content. Drafts, pending, private, trashed and password-protected
posts are never listed, whatever you choose in Settings.

What happens when I delete the plugin?

Everything it created is removed: both of its database tables (the crawler log and the MCP
access log), its MCP tokens, every option and cached value it wrote, and its scheduled
cleanup job. Deactivating the plugin, by contrast, leaves your
crawler history intact so you can switch it back on without losing anything.

Can I block AI crawlers like GPTBot?

Yes, if you choose to. Site Answers → Settings has a choice for every crawler it knows:
No change, Allow or Block. Block adds a Disallow: / rule for that crawler to your
robots.txt; Allow adds a rule inviting it in. Nothing changes until you choose, and each
crawler’s row says what it is for — some collect training data, others open your page only
when someone asks an AI assistant about it, and blocking those means the assistant cannot read
you when asked.

robots.txt is a request that well-behaved crawlers follow, not a lock. If your site has a
robots.txt file of its own on the server, WordPress’s robots.txt is never used, so the choices
cannot apply — the Settings screen tells you when that is the case.

Why does the Overview say my robots.txt blocks a crawler I never blocked?

Because something else did: another plugin, your host, or a line in a robots.txt file on your
server. The Overview reads the robots.txt your visitors actually get and names every AI
crawler it turns away, whoever wrote the rule. If you set a crawler to Allow and another rule
still blocks it, the Overview says that too.
sections.changelog:
1.1.1

  • The AI Agents (MCP) screen now carries the same “Get early access” link as the Overview. It is a plain link — the plugin still makes no outbound request.
  • New screenshots and banner showing the MCP server first.

1.1.0

  • New: a read-only MCP server (Model Context Protocol) at /wp-json/site-answers/v1/mcp, with four tools for AI agents: search_content, get_post, list_recent and get_site_info. Pages come back as clean Markdown. There are no write tools.
  • New: Site Answers → AI Agents (MCP). Make and revoke a token for each agent (only a fingerprint is stored), 60 calls a minute per token, and an access log of which token used which tool on which page, and when. No IP addresses.
  • New: on WordPress 6.9 and newer the same four tools are registered with the Abilities API, so the official MCP Adapter plugin offers them to signed-in agents. Can be switched off in Settings.
  • The plugin’s name is now “Site Answers – MCP Server, llms.txt & AI Crawler Log”.
  • The “llms.txt says not found” answer no longer suggests re-saving Permalinks, which cannot help: the plugin adds no rewrite rules.

1.0.2

  • New: a “Get early access” link at the foot of the Overview screen, for a possible paid add-on. It is a plain link — the plugin still makes no outbound request.

1.0.1

  • New: /llms-full.txt — the full text of every page in llms.txt, in one file. Same pages and exclusions, 5 MB cap, can be switched off.
  • New: the Overview says when your robots.txt asks an AI crawler to stay away, whoever wrote the rule.
  • New: allow or block each AI crawler in robots.txt from Settings. Nothing changes until you choose, and no file is written.
  • llms.txt now points to llms-full.txt while it is published.
  • Tested on every PHP version from 7.4 to 8.4 with WordPress 6.5, 6.8, 7.0 and 7.1.

1.0.0

  • First release.
  • Publishes /llms.txt from your published posts and pages, rebuilt automatically on publish, edit and delete.
  • Serves a clean Markdown copy of any post or page at the same address plus .md, and advertises it in a Link header.
  • Logs visits from 19 named AI crawlers, with the page requested and the response status.
  • Settings for content types, how many entries to list, and whether to honour “noindex”.
  • No external requests, no IP addresses, no telemetry.

short_description: A read-only MCP server for AI agents, plus llms.txt, Markdown pages and a log of which AI crawlers read your site. No account, no external service.

screenshots.caption: AI Agents (MCP): the MCP server address, a token for each AI agent, and the access log of which tool read which page, and when.
What an AI agent gets back over MCP: a real search_content and get_post answer from the demo site, as clean Markdown rather than page HTML.
The Overview: your llms.txt and llms-full.txt, whether your robots.txt lets AI crawlers in, which ones visited, and the pages they read most.
The llms.txt file itself, built from your own posts and pages.
Settings: which content is listed, the full-text file, the WordPress abilities switch, and an Allow / Block / No change choice for each AI crawler.
